summary: Describes how to produce digital signatures and hashes with the GOST R 34.10-2012 and GOST R 34.11-2012 algorithms for DNSKEY, RRSIG, and DS records in DNSSEC. It is informational, so it documents use of the algorithms rather than setting a standard.

eli5.summary: Domain name records can be stamped with a seal to prove they are real. This explains how to make that seal using Russia's national seal-making recipe.

questions: how to use gost algorithms in dnssec
subtitle: Securing the Domain Name System with Russian cryptographic standards

tldr.problem: Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) use digital signatures to prevent spoofing and tampering, but the standard algorithms may not be suitable for all regions or regulatory requirements, particularly those requiring Russian cryptographic standards.
tldr.mechanism: GOST R 34.10-2012 provides digital signatures and GOST R 34.11-2012 provides hashing. These Russian national standards can sign DNS resource records and can be stored in DNSKEY and DS records just like other algorithms.
tldr.outcome: DNS operators in Russia and countries requiring GOST compliance can use DNSSEC with their national cryptographic standards. However, this RFC is informational and not an IETF standard, and GOST has not been independently verified by the IETF.

today: RFC 9558 is an Informational RFC published as an independent submission. It is not an IETF standard, and support for GOST in DNSSEC is optional. The document remains relevant for organizations in Russia or those required by regulation to use GOST cryptography for DNSSEC, but it has not achieved widespread adoption in the global DNS infrastructure.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) is the global address book for the Internet. DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records, proving that they are authentic and have not been tampered with. RFC 4033, RFC 4034, and RFC 4035 describe the DNSSEC system and the algorithms that can be used to sign records.

This document extends the list of algorithms with Russian national standards: GOST R 34.10-2012 for digital signatures and GOST R 34.11-2012 for hashing. These are Russian government standards. The document specifies how to store GOST public keys in DNSKEY records, how to create RRSIG (signature) records, and how to use GOST digests in DS (Delegation Signer) records for DNSSEC.

Important caution: This RFC is informational, not a standard. It does not have IETF community consensus. The cryptographic properties of GOST have not been independently verified by the IETF or IRTF. The algorithms may contain weaknesses, either intentional or unintended. Support for GOST in DNSSEC-aware systems is optional.
sections.eli5: A recipe for making stamps exists. This document says how to use a different recipe—Russia's official recipe—to make DNS stamps that work the same way.

sections.title: GOST Keys and Signatures in DNSSEC
sections.content:
DNSSEC protects DNS by using pairs of cryptographic keys. A zone has two keys: a Key Signing Key (KSK) for signing other keys, and a Zone Signing Key (ZSK) for signing records in the zone. Public keys are stored in DNSKEY resource records. Signatures are stored in RRSIG (Resource Record Signature) records.

When you sign a zone with GOST, the process works the same as with other algorithms. A GOST public key is a point on an elliptic curve, represented as two 32-byte coordinates (x and y). The GOST signature algorithm takes the hash of the record to sign and produces a 512-bit (64-byte) signature using the GOST R 34.10-2012 algorithm. The hash is computed using GOST R 34.11-2012.

The main challenge is compatibility. Most DNS resolvers worldwide understand RSA and ECDSA signatures but not GOST. If you sign a zone with GOST alone, many resolvers will treat it as unsigned. Therefore, deployments should consider using dual algorithms: signing with both GOST and a widely-supported algorithm (like RSA or ECDSA) until GOST-aware DNSSEC software becomes more common.
sections.eli5: Two keys protect a zone: a master key and a working key. GOST lets you use a Russian recipe for both. But most people still use other recipes, so your zone should use both until everyone learns the Russian recipe.

sections.title: DNSKEY and RRSIG Records
sections.content:
GOST public keys in DNSKEY records use algorithm number 23. A GOST key is exactly 64 octets: the first 32 bytes are the x-coordinate of the elliptic curve point (in little-endian format), and the next 32 bytes are the y-coordinate (also little-endian). The document specifies which parameter set to use: parameter set A from RFC 7836, which defines a 256-bit variant of GOST for both signature and hash.

When signing an RRset (a group of records with the same name and type), the signer first computes the GOST R 34.11-2012 hash of the record data. Then it signs this hash using the GOST R 34.10-2012 algorithm. The resulting signature (64 bytes) is placed in the RRSIG record. The format is compatible with RFC 7091, which defines the wire format for GOST signatures.

To use GOST keys with standard cryptographic libraries, you may need to prepend 30 bytes of ASN.1 structure to the 64-byte key data. These bytes encode the parameter set and algorithm identifiers in X.509 format, allowing existing cryptographic toolkits to parse GOST keys correctly.
sections.eli5: A GOST key is 64 bytes: the secret lock shape written down. A signature is also 64 bytes: the result of signing with the secret. Some tools need you to add 30 bytes of instructions before the key so they know which recipe was used.

sections.title: Sizes and Specifications
sections.content:
This specification requires specific key and signature sizes. GOST R 34.10-2012 keys MUST be 512 bits (64 bytes) as defined in RFC 7091. Signatures produced by this algorithm MUST also be 512 bits. Hash digests produced by GOST R 34.11-2012 MUST be 256 bits (32 bytes) as defined in RFC 6986. These sizes are fixed and non-negotiable for this RFC.

In DS records, which contain a digest of the DNSKEY record for secure delegation, GOST R 34.11-2012 is registered as digest type 5. The 256-bit digest is placed in the DS record. This allows a parent zone to securely reference a child zone that uses GOST signatures by publishing a GOST digest of the child's DNSKEY record.

The RFC specifies that the 256-bit variants of both GOST algorithms be used. While RFC 6986 and RFC 7091 define longer variants (512-bit), this specification deliberately constrains implementations to the 256-bit versions for consistency and compatibility.
sections.eli5: The lock is 64 bytes. The key is 64 bytes. The digest is 32 bytes. These numbers are fixed so everyone's recipe gives the same result.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC carries a significant security note: GOST R 34.10-2012 and GOST R 34.11-2012 are Russian national standards whose cryptographic properties have not been independently verified by the IETF or IRTF. The algorithms may contain either intentional or unintended weaknesses. Implementers must be aware of this risk.

Like any cryptographic algorithm, GOST could be found to have a significant flaw in the future. If that happens, deployments should migrate to another algorithm. RFC 7583 provides guidance on the timing of such key rollovers. In the interim, it is recommended to use a dual-algorithm setup, signing zones with both GOST and a widely-supported algorithm (such as RSA or ECDSA), until GOST-aware DNSSEC software becomes more widespread.

RFC 6840 specifies that systems which do not support GOST algorithms MUST ignore associated RRSIG, DNSKEY, and DS records. This means zones signed only with GOST may appear unsigned to resolvers that do not support it, creating operational risks in mixed deployments.
sections.eli5: Nobody outside Russia has checked this recipe carefully. It could have a hidden flaw. Until many people use it, do not rely on it alone—use another recipe too.

sections.title: Practical Use and Limitations
sections.content:
This RFC documents how to use GOST algorithms in DNSSEC, but it is informational rather than a standard. Support for GOST in DNSSEC software is optional, not required. Implementers are not obligated to support it, and most DNS resolvers do not currently do so.

The RFC is useful for organizations required to use GOST by Russian law or regulation, or for zones operated in Russia where national cryptographic standards are mandated. For other organizations, GOST support in DNSSEC is not necessary. The document acknowledges this by noting that it is an independent submission, not a work of the IETF, and does not have the IETF's consensus or verification.

For anyone implementing GOST DNSSEC support, the RFC provides clear specifications: key format (64 octets), signature format (64 octets), digest type (5), and algorithm number (23). It also provides example DNSKEY, RRSIG, and DS records showing how GOST records look in practice.
sections.eli5: This is optional. Most of the world does not need it. If you are required to use Russia's recipe by law, here is how. Otherwise, the other recipes work fine.
